title: The bare bone
hookLine: sense pleasures satisfy like a bare bone to a hungry dog

lines: THAT ISN'T WHAT CUTTING OFF MEANS.
cards: Best clothes, a parasol, sandals: Potaliya, a householder, walks up to the Buddha dressed for an occasion. When the Buddha calls him householder, he bristles. I'm not a householder anymore, he says.
I've given my wealth to my children. I've cut myself off from all worldly affairs. I just live on food and clothing.
The Buddha says, gently: that isn't what cutting off means in this teaching. Potaliya wants to know what is.

teach.b: This is the fifty-fourth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse to Potaliya. Real cutting off, the Buddha says, is inward: giving up killing, stealing, lying, slander, greed, spite, anger and arrogance.
Then he turns to sense pleasures, with a run of pictures. The first is the one people remember. A dog, weak with hunger, waits by a butcher's shop.

teach.h: A HUNGRY DOG AND A BARE BONE
teach.b: The butcher throws it a bone scraped clean of meat, with only a smear of blood on it. The dog gnaws and gnaws. Does that bone take away its hunger?
No, says Potaliya. It only gets the dog tired and frustrated. Sense pleasures are like that bone, says the Buddha: much pain, much disappointment, more danger in them than delight.
They taste of something, and leave the hunger where it was. More pictures follow.

teach.h: A BIRD, A TORCH, A DREAM, A LOAN
teach.b: A bird flying off with a scrap of meat, chased by other birds who peck and claw at it until it lets go. A grass torch carried into the wind, burning the hand that holds it. A dream of a lovely park, gone when you wake.
Goods borrowed for show, which the owners come and take back. Notice what he isn't saying. He isn't saying the bone is evil, or that a dog is foolish to want food.

teach.h: SOME THINGS ONLY LOOK LIKE FOOD
teach.b: Some things only look like food: you can gnaw them all day and stay hungry.
And Potaliya, who came in claiming he had cut everything off, finds he had only cut off his wealth.

how: Some Buddhist teachers use MN 54's similes, such as the bare bone and the grass torch, in reflections on the drawbacks of sense pleasures, pointing practitioners toward a deeper contentment in meditation and ethical living.

o: a hungry dog waiting outside a butcher's
a householder who said he'd given it all up
a monk who handed his wealth to the poor

games.q: the pictures of pleasure — tap the pairs.
p: gnawed by a dog, leaves it hungry
a bird chased and pecked by others
carried into the wind, burns the hand
the owners come and take them back

s: the Buddha says wanting food is foolish
hunger is real; the point is that some things only look like food and leave us hungry.
Potaliya said he had cut off all worldly affairs
and the Buddha told him real cutting off is inward: giving up killing, lying, greed, anger and arrogance.
the dog's bone was scraped clean of meat
only a smear of blood was left on it: it tasted of something, and couldn't fill the dog.

games.q: you're Potaliya. you've given your wealth to your children and say you've cut off all worldly affairs. the Buddha says that isn't cutting off. what do you do?
o: ask what cutting off means in his teaching.
games.why: Potaliya asks. the Buddha explains that real cutting off is inward, then gives the similes of the bone, the bird, the torch, the dream and the loan.

practice: Think of something you return to again and again, hoping it'll fill you, scrolling, snacking, checking, shopping, replaying an argument, and picture the last time: did it take the hunger away, or leave you tired?
Don't scold yourself; a hungry dog isn't bad. Just see the bone clearly, ask what real food for that hunger would be, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Potaliya. The householder who heard of a bone scraped clean, thrown to a hungry dog: something that tastes like food and leaves you hungry.

carryVoice: Your line: a bare bone. It tastes of something, and the hunger stays. That's day four hundred forty-six.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 54, Potaliya Sutta (the discourse to Potaliya)
Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (list of similes for sense pleasures)
